articles.title: Shipping fuel shocks could hit consumer prices in vulnerable economies nearly twice as hard
articles.summary: A sustained 70–80% rise in maritime fuel costs could increase consumer prices by 0.35% in least developed countries (LDCs), almost twice the global average of 0.19%. Small island developing states (SIDS) could also face disproportionate impacts, with consumer prices estimated to rise by 0.27%, according to the Review...
articles.body: Shipping fuel shocks could hit consumer prices in vulnerable economies nearly twice as hard in International Shipping News 27/11/2026 A sustained 70–80% rise in maritime fuel costs could increase consumer prices by 0.35% in least developed countries (LDCs), almost twice the global average of 0.19%. Small island developing states (SIDS) could also face disproportionate impacts, with consumer prices estimated to rise by 0.27%, according to the Review of Maritime Transport 2026, published by UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD) on 26 November. The projections reflect how higher maritime fuel costs, following disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, could affect consumer prices. The estimated increase is comparable to the rise in average maritime fuel costs between January–February and March–June 2026, assuming that higher costs are sustained through the end of 2027. How shipping costs feed through to consumers Maritime fuel or bunker fuel is a major operating cost for shipping companies. When fuel prices rise, so can the cost of transporting goods, including imported consumer goods and production inputs, eventually feeding through to consumer prices. The simulations in the report isolate the impact of higher maritime fuel costs, while excluding the broader economic effects of general oil price increases. The overall impact of an energy price shock could therefore be greater. Why LDCs and SIDS are more exposed LDCs continue to lag significantly behind the rest of the world in liner shipping connectivity, despite having improved their liner shipping connectivity about three times faster over the past two decades. These economies, along with SIDS, are particularly exposed because their imports often travel along longer, indirect routes through transshipment hubs. This increases cumulative fuel consumption and leaves them with few alternatives when shipping routes are disrupted. Their greater reliance on imported goods for consumption and domestic production has also been a factor. Heavy imports of often lower-value goods tend to incur higher fuel costs relative to their value. How to strengthen resilience Higher shipping costs can make essential imports less affordable, raise costs for businesses and reduce households’ purchasing power, the report warns. It calls for closer monitoring of freight markets and shipping costs, better assessment of their implications, as well as stronger capacity in developing countries to respond to rising transport costs. It also recommends coordinating advance planning to manage multi-hazard disruptions, investment in sustainable and resilient ports and logistics networks, as well as enhanced trade facilitation to ensure that goods continue to move reliably and affordably across supply chains. Equally important is the need to mitigate shipping cost increases by improving efficiency, sustainability and resilience. More energy-efficient ships and a shift to cleaner fuels can help decarbonize shipping and reduce the sector’s exposure to volatile fossil fuel prices. These efforts will be crucial to helping vulnerable economies, particularly LDCs and SIDS, maintain access to essential goods and reducing the risks of future disruptions deepening existing vulnerabilities. articles.title: UK port congestion, empty-container restrictions add upward pressure to freight rates
articles.summary: Congestion across the UK container logistics network is tightening effective vessel and equipment capacity, adding upward pressure to freight prices as carriers contend with import backlogs, schedule disruption and restrictions on empty-container returns. Maersk said in a Nov. 24 customer advisory that sustained high...
articles.body: UK port congestion, empty-container restrictions add upward pressure to freight rates in International Shipping News 27/11/2026 Congestion across the UK container logistics network is tightening effective vessel and equipment capacity, adding upward pressure to freight prices as carriers contend with import backlogs, schedule disruption and restrictions on empty-container returns. Maersk said in a Nov. 24 customer advisory that sustained high import volumes, network congestion, adverse weather and recent rail disruption had placed pressure on UK and Ireland port and landside operations. Vessel delays and high use of inland storage were compounding the disruption, with the carrier warning that normal network fluidity would take time to restore despite services beginning to recover. Empty-equipment bottlenecks have become an additional constraint. London Gateway stopped accepting empty-container returns Nov. 24, Maersk said in a separate customer advisory, while Felixstowe Quay and Tilbury Quay remained closed to empties pending planned evacuation operations. The restrictions risk extending truck turn times and repositioning distances while reducing the speed at which equipment can be returned to circulation. This could effectively remove capacity from the market even where nominal vessel space remains available. Market participants said the disruption was most pronounced in North Europe but could affect pricing and capacity management across wider European trades. “I think [North Europe and UK] has more congestion issues versus [the Mediterranean], but it still causes issues across each region,” a container operator said. The operator attributed the persistent congestion to insufficient manpower, delayed infrastructure improvements and vessels arriving outside their scheduled berth windows. The operator said the problems had been developing for more than a year and that recently announced blank sailings could provide some operational breathing room but “will not cure the problem.” “Definitely congestion is an issue. When demand picks up more, congestion will get worse,” an agent said, adding that recently announced blank sailings would reduce available space. The possible return of more Asia-Europe services to Suez Canal routings could create another near-term operational challenge. While shorter routings would eventually release vessel capacity compared with longer voyages around southern Africa, a forwarder said the transition could initially worsen congestion as schedules are reset and vessel arrivals become concentrated. “In the short term it will drive more congestion,” a forwarder said. The combination of delayed vessels, constrained terminal storage, inland disruption and limits on empty returns is reducing effective capacity at multiple points in the supply chain. With blank sailings further narrowing available vessel space, UK congestion is expected to remain a source of upward pressure on freight prices until terminals clear backlogs and empty equipment begins circulating more normally. Platts Container Rate 1 (PCR1) – North Asia to North Europe – and Platts Container Rate 11 (PCR11) – North Asia to the UK – were last assessed Nov. 24 at $3,400 per FEU. Platts Container Rate 3 (PCR3) – North Asia to the Mediterranean – was assessed at $5,400 per FEU. Platts is part of S&P Global Energy. Source: Platts 2026-11-27 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: BIMCO regrets European Parliament vote to exclude Indian yards
articles.summary: BIMCO is concerned by the European Parliament’s decision on 25 November to reject the inclusion of two Indian yards on the European List of ship recycling facilities. The two yards have undergone an extensive, independent inspection process carried out by the EU Commission, the results of which are publicly available...
articles.body: BIMCO regrets European Parliament vote to exclude Indian yards in International Shipping News 27/11/2026 BIMCO is concerned by the European Parliament’s decision on 25 November to reject the inclusion of two Indian yards on the European List of ship recycling facilities. The two yards have undergone an extensive, independent inspection process carried out by the EU Commission, the results of which are publicly available in the Commission’s inspection reports. The Commission’s inspection process confirmed that both yards meet the requirements of the EU Ship Recycling Regulation (EU SRR) and its Technical Guidance Note. The decision by EU parliament to object to the inclusion of the two yards in the EU list ignores the evidence. Inclusion on the list should rest on whether a facility meets the EU’s safety and environmental requirements. By setting aside the Commission’s findings, the Parliament undermines the credibility of the EU’s own legislation. It also fails to recognise years of substantial investment by the yards in infrastructure, safety systems and environmental management since the adoption of the IMO Hong Kong Convention in 2009. This outcome turns the EU SRR process into a political, opaque and unreliable framework, which is the last thing the global shipping industry needs. Shipowners need a predictable, fact-based framework that lists compliant yards on their merits. BIMCO believes this is why the IMO Hong Kong Convention (HKC) should be the single global instrument as it places responsibilities with the respective authorities: the recycling state, the flag and the port state. By rejecting the inclusion of compliant Indian yards, the EU Parliament fails to deliver an outcome based on facts, by ignoring the EU’s own inspection processes and conclusions. Note: The final decision on the European List will now be taken by the European Commission, after the 27 EU Member States have been given the opportunity to vote on the inclusion of the yards. Source: BIMCO, https://www.bimco.org/news-insights/bimco-news/2026/11/25-eu-vote/ 2026-11-27 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: Understanding current regulatory requirements shaping battery-powered vessel design
articles.summary: Summary • There is currently no global regulatory framework governing requirements for battery-powered vessels, with classification societies stepping in to fill the gap • While classification societies share a common focus on safety, requirements and guidelines vary across societies • System redundancy is a key...
articles.body: Understanding current regulatory requirements shaping battery-powered vessel design in International Shipping News , Shipping: Emission Possible 27/11/2026 Summary • There is currently no global regulatory framework governing requirements for battery-powered vessels, with classification societies stepping in to fill the gap • While classification societies share a common focus on safety, requirements and guidelines vary across societies • System redundancy is a key principle for maintaining the safety and functionality of battery-powered vessels • Managing the risks of thermal runaway requires careful design, as mitigation of some hazards can increase the risk of others • Design should protect batteries and battery spaces from damage, including from collisions and the entry of solids or liquids • Battery spaces should be arranged to minimize and contain the risk of fires • Classification societies have developed specific requirements for the certification, control, and monitoring of battery systems • Flag states may have additional requirements, such as specific processes for risk assessment and design review Why regulatory requirements matter for scalability of battery-electric propulsion Scalability depends not only on technical performance, but also on regulatory, operational, infrastructure, and economic considerations.1 This article focuses on some of the regulatory requirements that influence the deployment of battery-vessels, complementing our report on ‘Battery-electric propulsion: Technical maturity and scalability across shipping segments’.2 Although various battery chemistries are available, we focus primarily on lithium-ion battery systems, which are currently the most popular choice for ship operators.3 Due to its high energy density, nickel manganese cobalt (NMC) is currently the dominant lithium-ion chemistry in the battery-powered fleet, particularly in applications where weight and space are constrained. For a shipowner or designer considering the technical feasibility of battery-electrification, understanding whether a battery system can meet the vessel’s energy demand is only part of the picture. The requirements set by classification societies and flag states also directly shape how battery systems can be designed, arranged, and certified on board. At present, there is no single international framework for these regulatory requirements, complicating the adoption process for shipowners and designers. This lack of standardization is itself one of the parameters shaping how quickly this technology can be adopted at scale. The existing regulatory landscape To date, classification societies have played a key role in supporting the safe adoption of battery-powered vessels. Several societies have published extensive requirements, with particular emphasis on lithium-ion chemistries and hybrid arrangements. At the time of writing, the International Maritime Organization (IMO) has not published dedicated requirements governing battery-powered propulsion systems. The IMO Subcommittee on Ship Systems and Equipment has started work on interim guidelines for the safety of ships using battery energy storage systems, slated for completion in 2028.4 In the absence of a common regulatory approach, battery system requirements have so far evolved through individual classification society frameworks. For the purposes of this article, we reviewed the published requirements for battery-powered vessels issued by five classification societies.5, 6, 7, 8, 9 While the requirements show some variation, they converge on a common overriding objective: the battery energy storage system (referred to here as the battery system) space shall be arranged such that an incident within the system will not endanger the safety of passengers, crew, or vessel. Many classification societies impose dedicated requirements on lithium-ion battery installations used as a source of electrical power when their rated energy capacity exceeds a specified threshold. The threshold is commonly 20 kWh, although it may be applied per battery system installation or battery space room, depending on the classification society.5, 6, 8, 10 The threshold is based on National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) Standard 855 and the International Fire Code (IFC), with the primary intent of facilitating containment of the system in the event of an incident. Battery systems used in marine applications are typically well above this level, often by one or more orders of magnitude. Above the threshold, the rules extend beyond control and protection functions to cover the installation arrangement and location of the batteries themselves. Redundancy as a design requirement Redundancy means that the ship’s electrical system is configured with independent backup arrangements, so that the failure of one part does not result in the loss of propulsion or other essential services. In practice, this requires both physical and electrical independence, so that a single fault or other casualty affecting one system does not simultaneously disable its backup. Electrical independence is usually achieved by giving each battery system its own switchboard, or in some cases by splitting the main switchboard into at least two sections linked by circuit breakers (Figure 1). Physical independence is usually achieved by placing each system in its own compartment with fire-rated boundaries and by keeping their auxiliary services (e.g., ventilation, off-gas exhaust, gas detection, fire detection and fire extinguishing arrangements) separate rather than shared. Thermal runaway Thermal runaway occurs when the rate of heat generation within a battery cell exceeds its heat-dissipation capacity, causing a self-sustaining temperature rise that can lead to fire, explosion, and the release of toxic off-gases.4 Depending on the cell chemistry and installation, any of these hazards may pose the greatest risk. What makes thermal runaway difficult to design against is that measures used to mitigate one hazard may intensify another, creating a trade-off between ventilation and firefighting strategies. Ventilation helps remove flammable and toxic off-gases, reducing the risk of gas accumulation and explosion, but it can also supply oxygen that supports combustion. Conversely, isolating the space can limit oxygen availability and reduce fire risk, but may allow flammable gases to accumulate and reach explosive concentrations within the enclosure. The consequences of thermal runaway risk extend beyond the battery itself and must be considered in the overall arrangement of the vessel. To meet this requirement, the design must account for both normal operation and operation after a single failure.5, 6 The redundant energy source must meet the power demand in both of these scenarios, although a limited reduction in propulsion capability may be acceptable if overall vessel safety is maintained. Two measures can help facilitate compliance with these criteria. The first is further subdivision, which improves redundancy by distributing the installed energy across a greater number of independent battery systems located in separate spaces. The second is vessel speed: because the relationship between ship speed and required power is non-linear, a given percentage reduction in speed produces a proportionally larger reduction in power demand.13 Accepting a lower operating speed therefore reduces the vessel’s power and energy demand, making the redundancy criteria considerably easier to meet. By contrast, in hybrid electric vessels, the battery is typically complemented with an onboard combustion-based generation source. For these vessels, redundancy can be addressed at the level of the overall power system rather than solely through independent battery arrangements. Location and protection of battery spaces Classification society requirements for the location and protection of battery spaces include: Location Battery spaces must be located aft of the collision bulkhead5, 6, 8, 10 and are not to be contiguous with the vessel’s side or bottom shell. This protects the battery spaces from collision or grounding damage. For small vessels and tugs this may be relaxed subject to a risk assessment. Ingress protection (IP) The IP rating, in accordance with IEC 60529,14 describes an enclosure’s resistance to the ingress of solid objects and liquids. The minimum required IP rating of a battery system enclosure depends on the installation location, environmental conditions, and applicable classification society requirements. The highest levels of protection are typically required where water ingress, immersion, or significant environmental exposure may occur. Some classification societies specify IP44 as the minimum required level of protection.5, 6, 7 Higher ratings apply in more demanding conditions, such as IP67 for open-deck enclosures only under specific classification requirements. Boundary integrity Space boundaries must be gastight to adjacent compartments and watertight below the vessel’s damaged waterline.5, 6 Where spaces are below the vessel’s damage waterline, an IPX7 rating may be accepted where the space is not completely watertight.5 Under another class’s requirements, an IPX7 rating may be required if battery systems are installed below the freeboard deck. Fire safety Battery housing spaces are typically arranged within dedicated enclosed compartments that are separated from adjacent spaces and intended to contain a fire within the space of origin. Depending on the applicable class rules, battery capacity and system function, they may be treated either as machinery spaces other than Category A or as Category A machinery spaces (as specified in SOLAS Regulation II-2)15 for specific fire-safety requirements.5, 6 In practice, this typically requires fire-insulated boundaries, with ratings such as A-60 depending on the battery space classification, applicable rules, and adjacent spaces. Containerized battery systems The same containment logic extends to containerized systems, where the format itself introduces additional handling and arrangement requirements. Three container types are distinguished: (i) fixed, permanently integrated with the vessel and replaced only at end of life (ii) flexible, kept on board to charge and discharged in place but removable when required (iii) swappable (portable), exchanged for a pre-charged container after each discharge Fixed and flexible units are recharged in place, typically from shore power, whereas swappable units are lifted off and replaced with pre-charged containers. Across all types, the container’s safety functions (battery management, gas detection, emergency disconnect) stay powered in all operational modes, with state of charge monitored throughout storage, handling and use, not only when connected to the ship.5 Swapping is well suited to short-route vessels with limited port stay times and reduces grid impacts, as battery containers can be recharged onshore during off-peak periods or using renewable electricity.18 However, this solution requires specialized crane infrastructure and handling and transport of heavy battery containers. Together with the additional battery inventory and associated costs and logistics requirements, these needs have so far limited the adoption of swappable batteries across the shipping sector. Class requirements may further prohibit container stacking (unless justified by risk assessment) and specify the following requirements for the container: • Normally unmanned • Fire-rated boundaries that contain a fire within the space of origin • Protection against sea, icing and physical damage, including suitable IP rating Certification, control, and monitoring Classification societies have specified several requirements that apply well to certification, control, and monitoring of battery systems: Cells and batteries Cells and batteries are to be designed, type-tested and certified to IEC 62619 20 (safety under abnormal operating conditions) and IEC 62620 21 (performance and endurance), or recognized equivalents. Battery management system A battery management system is required to monitor and control the cells, perform cell balancing to maintain uniform state of charge across cells, and cut off on overcharge, overcurrent, over-discharge or overheating. Energy management system An energy management system is required to monitor the battery system’s available energy and power and manage its use so that sufficient power remains available for operation.5, 6, 7, 8, 10 Sometimes, this functionality may be integrated with another system, e.g. the power management system. State monitoring State of charge and state of health are to be monitored at a manned control station.5, 6, 10 State of health is additionally verified periodically, for example by coulomb counting over a full charge or discharge cycle (or similar method). Flag state considerations While class rules provide the technical basis for design and approval, the flag state retains statutory authority and may impose additional requirements for battery installations. Some flag state administrations have issued their own guidance on lithium-ion battery installations, which may call for a risk assessment and dedicated design review as part of the approval process for lithium-ion battery installations.22, 23 Such guidance generally supplements the class rules rather than replacing them, and its scope varies between administrations. The applicable flag state requirements should be confirmed early alongside the relevant class rules. While this independent work has been valuable in building early experience, it also highlights the need for greater standardization across the industry to ensure the technology can scale up effectively. Source: Mærsk Mc-Kinney Møller Center for Zero Carbon Shipping 2026-11-27 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share
takeaways: For a shipowner or designer considering the technical feasibility of battery-electrification, understanding whether a battery system can meet the vessel’s energy demand is only part of the picture.
The requirements set by classification societies and flag states also directly shape how battery systems can be designed, arranged, and certified on board.
At present, there is no single international framework for these regulatory requirements, complicating the adoption process for shipowners and designers.

articles.body: AI money keeps flowing into logistics, but a softer 2027 freight market will demand proof, says Deep Current in International Shipping News 27/11/2026 Dealmaking in logistics technology surged in 2026 and funding is on course to rise, but a softer 2027 freight market will reward only the AI that is embedded in clear workflows and delivers measurable savings, according to the year-end outlook from Deep Current AS, the Norwegian logistics AI company. That is a central finding of a new industry study conducted by Deep Current AS, examining how logistics and maritime businesses approached technology adoption in 2026 and the priorities likely to shape implementation in 2027. The study draws on conversations with senior executives from logistics, shipping and maritime companies, supported by company disclosures, annual and financial reports, technology investment announcements and industry research. It examines developments across freight forwarding, container shipping, warehousing, port operations, logistics services and supply-chain technology. “AI has to get smarter in 2027, and smarter means embedded,” said Tamim Fannoush, founder and CEO of Deep Current. “The companies that benefit next year will be the ones whose AI sits inside a clear workflow, moves work from one step to the next and makes it obvious who does what. Too much AI without a clear pathway to an efficient workflow only adds clutter and confusion. Forwarders will keep the tools that make the next step obvious and drop the rest.” Interest is high, proof is thinner Funding to supply chain management and logistics start-ups reached $8.4 billion by mid-August, putting 2026 on course to pass the $9 billion raised in 2025. Deal-making accelerated too, with Capstone Partners counting 66 logistics technology M&A transactions by mid-October, up 73.7% year on year. Deep Current surveyed CEOs of top European shipping and maritime companies. One of the respondents, Sogese S.r.l, an Italian company operating in the cold storage and container storage sectors with a strong focus on the European market, has progressively moved towards a more data-driven business model over the past three years, with developments across ERP processes, fleet and inventory management, business intelligence and digital customer engagement. AI is emerging as an additional tool to support commercial activities, market analysis and strategic decision-making. “Technology has made the greatest difference in asset visibility, inventory management and our ability to analyse operational and financial performance,” said Andrea Sogese, CEO of Sogese. “But the main challenges are organisational culture, employee adoption and data quality, rather than the technology itself. Data cleansing, validation and standardisation are essential before introducing automation or AI into existing business processes. Without these foundations, even sophisticated technologies can generate misleading or operationally unusable outputs.” For businesses managing physical assets and storage infrastructure, the value of technology extends beyond automation. Reliable data can influence decisions on asset utilisation, inventory management, procurement, pricing and capacity planning. Digitalisation can improve information sharing across departments, but its value depends on whether the information being shared is consistent and usable. “The question from forwarders used to be whether AI works. In 2026 it became where AI pays back,” Fannoush said. “Investors are funding tools that do operational work, and buyers now want the saving to show up in their numbers.” A tighter market sharpens the test Deep Current’s outlook sets the technology investment story against a container market sending mixed signals. US container imports hit a record 2.675 million TEU in October, up 16% year on year according to Descartes Datamyne, yet Drewry’s World Container Index fell 3% to $4,176 per FEU on 19 November. Carriers are returning to the Suez Canal, which can release capacity without a single new ship, and Danish Ship Finance puts scheduled container fleet additions in 2027–2029 at 32% of the existing fleet. These developments will put additional pressure on freight economics and make operational efficiency more important. In a tighter commercial environment, the ability to identify errors, manage assets and make informed decisions using reliable information becomes increasingly valuable. “A softer freight market removes the margin that used to absorb errors,” Fannoush said. “When a booking, a dangerous goods declaration or a quote carries a mistake into operations, the carrier, the terminal and the customer all see it. The AI that earns its place in 2027 is the AI that catches those errors before the shipment moves.” For Sogese, the next phase of technology adoption will involve greater integration between business platforms, stronger data governance and more extensive use of AI-assisted decision-making. “We are seeing a gradual shift from basic digitalisation towards automation, AI and greater integration between business platforms. However, technological adoption is often progressing faster than data governance and organisational readiness,” Andrea Sogese said. “The real competitive advantage will come from combining technology, reliable data and a corporate culture capable of translating digital capabilities into measurable business improvements.” What Deep Current is watching in 2027 • Proof of return. Whether buyers ask for measured savings and vendors can show them, with unclear ROI still one of the most frequently cited barriers to adoption. • Workflow embedding. Whether AI is built into booking, documentation and quoting workflows with a clear path to efficiency, or sits beside them as one more tool to manage. • Data quality at the front end. Whether bookings, documents, dangerous goods declarations and quotes are validated before operations begin. • Consolidation. Whether deal volume holds and how acquirers integrate the AI platforms they buy. • Capacity. Actual Suez service restorations, deliveries against the orderbook, and whether December rate increases hold beyond their announced dates. • Geopolitics and infrastructure. Security in the Red Sea and the Strait of Hormuz, port congestion and labour negotiations. Beyond these developments, the ability of logistics businesses to integrate systems and establish reliable data foundations will remain an important factor in determining how effectively they can adopt AI. For European logistics companies, Sogese sees particular potential in predictive analytics, fleet optimisation, demand forecasting and commercial intelligence, provided the underlying data is reliable. “Information quality, interoperability, real-time visibility and cybersecurity will become increasingly important competitive factors for European logistics businesses,” Andrea Sogese said. “Our priorities will increasingly focus on system integration, data governance, business intelligence, AI-assisted decision-making and operational automation.” “Capital is plentiful in logistics technology. Evidence is scarcer,” Fannoush said. “The companies that publish measured results and fix data before cargo moves will win the 2027 budgets.” Source: Deep Current 2026-11-27 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: Why the Mediterranean is a hotspot for oil spills after tanker sinks near Ibiza
articles.summary: Spanish authorities are scrambling to contain any damage to its “vulnerable” Mediterranean waters following a huge oil spill. On Thursday (26 November), a tanker carrying up to 7,000 tonnes of diesel sank off the coast of Ibiza, leaving one dead. The Maltese-flagged Med Emre was travelling from the southern port of...
articles.body: Why the Mediterranean is a hotspot for oil spills after tanker sinks near Ibiza in International Shipping News 27/11/2026 Spanish authorities are scrambling to contain any damage to its “vulnerable” Mediterranean waters following a huge oil spill. On Thursday (26 November), a tanker carrying up to 7,000 tonnes of diesel sank off the coast of Ibiza, leaving one dead. The Maltese-flagged Med Emre was travelling from the southern port of Algeciras to Barcelona when it sank in the early hours of the morning. 17 crew members were rescued but one was later confirmed dead in hospital. According to maritime data tracking firm Kpler, the vessel was transporting around 66,000 barrels of refined products. It is currently unclear what caused the sinking. A government mechanism designed for marine pollution events had been activated, “but this does not presuppose that pollution has been detected on the coast”, Spanish government sources told news agency AFP. A boat and a plane belonging to Spanish maritime rescue service Salvamento Maritimo had been sent to assess the possible environmental damage, the Balearic emergency services added. The Civil Protection authority had requested the activation of the European Union’s Earth monitoring system Copernicus to obtain images of the area, said the government sources. ‘Amplified’ potential for pollution Maritime security expert Emilio Rodriguez Diaz from the University of Cadiz told local news that the area affected by the oil spill was “particularly vulnerable”. Any pollution entering the water could have a possible impact on tourism and on Mediterranean seagrasses that absorb substantial quantities of climate-heating carbon dioxide. Mediterranean seagrass acts as a major blue carbon sink, trapping carbon in deep rhizome and sediment layers while oxygenating coastal waters – but warming waters from climate change is already fuelling their demise. The area also includes spaces protected by the European Union’s Natura 2000 network and hosts the critically endangered Balearic Shearwater, says SEOBirdLife. “Contact with the fuel may alter the impermeability and the thermal insulation of the birds’ plumage, causing heat loss and hypothermia,” the NGO warned. Marine conservation group Oceana noted that the time of year was “key” for migratory species, including turtles, sharks, red tuna, pilot whales and the striped dolphin. Oil spills are one of the most concerning sources of marine pollution as they’re difficult to clean up and can last for a long time. “They can severely pollute marine and coastal habitats, causing damage to the natural environment and the economy,” says the European Environment Agency. “The Mediterranean Sea’s highly industrialised nature, characterised by the many extensive ports, refineries and petrochemical plants along its coastlines, amplifies the potential for pollution incidents.” Spain’s worst oil spill But Diaz downplayed comparisons to the 2002 Prestige oil disaster, Spain’s worst environmental accident so far. That spilled more than 60,000 tonnes of fuel and blackened thousands of kilometres of Atlantic coastline, affecting Spain, Portugal and France. The Med Emre was a modern ship, built in Turkey in 2019, with a double hull to ensure that, “in the event of a leak (or) a collision, that intermediate part between the cargo hold and the outer layer would flood”, he said. “It’s a kind of buffer that prevents the cargo… from being released into the environment.” In December 2024, a US-sanctioned Russian cargo ship sank in international waters off Spain’s southern Mediterranean coast with 16 people on board — two of whom were never found. A Spanish government letter to parliament earlier this year revealed the ship was transporting “components of two nuclear reactors similar to those used by submarines”. The vessel’s owner, a company that belongs to the Russian defence ministry, denounced at the time “a targeted terrorist attack”, without providing evidence. Source: Euronews 2026-11-27 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: Force Technology, Hempel and Teekay Step Up Vessel Performance Collaboration

articles.body: Force Technology, Hempel and Teekay Step Up Vessel Performance Collaboration in International Shipping News 27/11/2026 Force Technology has extended its long-standing partnership with marine coatings manufacturer Hempel A/S and shipowner Teekay, to advance data-driven vessel performance monitoring with focus on measurement and verification of fuel efficiency gains and emissions performance. Established in 2017, the collaboration leverages Force Technology’s SeaTrend vessel performance monitoring platform, which is commercially available to shipowners and operators worldwide, to provide consistent, data-based insights into vessel efficiency, hull condition and the operational impact of antifouling coatings across Teekay’s fleet. The renewed agreement will see the partners build on Hempel’s coating expertise, Teekay’s operational experience and Force Technology’s hydrodynamic modelling capabilities to drive smarter, data-led decision-making across fleet operations. SeaTrend continuously collects and analyses operational vessel data, enabling shipowners and operators to measure changes in performance over time, identify opportunities to improve fuel efficiency and assess the performance of hull coatings and maintenance strategies. The platform uses advanced hydrodynamic models developed through decades of maritime research and engineering experience to normalise data and provide consistent performance assessments. Supporting decarbonisation objectives through data With increasing pressure on the maritime industry to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and improve energy efficiency, accurate performance monitoring has become a valuable tool for identifying and documenting operational efficiency improvements. Through SeaTrends, Force Technology provides actionable insights that support the identification of opportunities to reduce fuel consumption and associated emissions, improved understanding of the effects of hull and propeller fouling, assess coating performance over time, and collect data and documentation to meet evolving environmental regulations. Industry partnership delivers operational value The extended partnership demonstrates how ship operators, technology providers and coating manufacturers can work together to identify opportunities to improve operational efficiency while supporting decarbonisation objectives. “Reliable performance data is essential for enabling better operational decisions and documenting efficiency improvements throughout a vessel’s lifecycle. Through this collaboration, we can combine advanced performance analytics with practical maritime expertise to deliver tangible value to vessel owners and operators,” says Jan Kastebo Michelsen, Director, Maritime & Civil Engineering at Force Technology. Marco Di Masa, Sales Manager – Marine, Hempel said: “Through our collaboration with Force Technology and Teekay, we can use operational data to assess the performance of our silicone-based Hempaguard hull coating across Teekay’s fleet. This enables our teams to proactively monitor fleet performance and support our customers in more informed coating and maintenance decisions.” George Mathew, Technical Manager, Teekay said: “Our fleet is built for the long term, and having a precise understanding of its performance is key. This partnership gives us a clear, independent view from real operations that helps us make better decisions on coatings, maintenance, and voyages well ahead of regulation.” As digitalisation and the shift towards lower-emission operations continue to reshape the maritime industry, Hempel, Teekay and Force Technology will explore further opportunities for collaboration to address the diverse vessel performance and environmental challenges faced by modern shipping. articles.title: K-Shipbuilding Shaken by China Even in High Value-Added Vessels
articles.summary: The South Korean shipbuilding industry, which has long solidified its position as a global ‘shipbuilding powerhouse’, stands at a major crossroads. Pushed back by China’s fierce offensive backed by the government’s full financial and policy support and strong price competitiveness, the market share gap in the high...
articles.body: K-Shipbuilding Shaken by China Even in High Value-Added Vessels in Shipbuilding News 27/11/2026 The South Korean shipbuilding industry, which has long solidified its position as a global ‘shipbuilding powerhouse’, stands at a major crossroads. Pushed back by China’s fierce offensive backed by the government’s full financial and policy support and strong price competitiveness, the market share gap in the high value-added vessel market is widening uncontrollably. As even the ultra-large container ship and liquefied natural gas (LNG) carrier markets, where domestic shipbuilders previously practically ran alone based on overwhelming technological superiority, are being rapidly chased by China, the dominant analysis is that a red light has turned on for the sustainability of K-Shipbuilding. According to Clarkson Research, a British shipbuilding and shipping market analysis agency, on Nov. 24, China won orders for a whopping 93 vessels in the global ultra-large container ship (15,000 TEU or more) market from January to October this year, while South Korea only managed to secure 6 vessels. Converting this into market share yields a shocking report card of 94% for China and 6% for South Korea. If South Korea fails to secure additional orders under this trend, it will record the lowest order market share in the recent 5 years (2022 to 2026). Ultra-large container ships, the flagship vessel type of global trade, are the second most expensive high value-added vessels after LNG carriers. As of the end of October, the newbuilding price for a 22,000 to 24,000 TEU class vessel reaches $240,000,000. This is a field where South Korea (21 vessels) held the upper hand over China (16 vessels) just a few years ago in 2023, but the tide has completely turned this year. In fact, in the bidding wars of major global shipping companies, the three major domestic shipbuilders (HD Hyundai Heavy Industries, Hanwha Ocean, and Samsung Heavy Industries) have suffered consecutive defeats to China. The winner of the order battle for 12 ultra-large container ships placed by France’s CMA-CGM, the world’s third-largest shipping company, last year was also China’s Yangzijiang Shipbuilding, not the domestic Big 3. Threat Even to the LNG Carrier Market, Called a ‘Home Turf’ A bigger problem is that even the LNG carrier market, the core of high value-added vessels, is facing a fierce pursuit by China. Of the 76 large LNG carrier orders worldwide from January to October this year, South Korea secured 44 vessels (57.9%) to maintain the lead, but China swept up a whopping 32 vessels (42.1%). This is a figure that surged more than 10 times compared to China’s total LNG carrier order volume (3 vessels) last year, and the market share gap with South Korea narrowed to a mere 15.8%p difference. The domestic industry is somewhat downgrading the increase in China’s LNG carrier orders, stating, “A significant number are internal projects associated with China’s own shippers,” but concerns are growing that if Chinese-made LNG carriers delivered in the future are proven to be flawless in actual operation, global shipping companies could massively and more rapidly defect to China. Shadow of the ‘Selective Order Strategy’ vs China’s Low-Price Offensive and Quality Improvement Regarding the background of domestic shipbuilders receiving such a sluggish report card, the industry diagnoses that complex causes have acted. First, as domestic shipbuilders have already amply secured more than 3 years of work (order backlog) through aggressive orders over the recent 2 to 3 years, they are concentrating their capabilities on relatively more profitable LNG carriers to efficiently utilize limited construction slots (docks). In other words, the analysis is that the shortage of docks and the profitability-oriented selective strategy led to the decrease in ultra-large container ship orders. At the same time, the remarkable improvement in the competitiveness of the Chinese shipbuilding industry is cited as a major cause. Beyond a simple avoidance phenomenon, it cannot be overlooked that the quality of the Chinese shipbuilding industry has improved to an extent incomparable to the past. Lastly, Yang Jong-seo, a visiting professor at the Department of Naval Architecture and Ocean Engineering at Seoul National University, pointed out, “Although China’s labor costs have also risen compared to the past, they are maintaining overwhelming price competitiveness based on continuous and full support from the government,” adding, “Unless the price gap narrows, it will be difficult for South Korea to maintain its advantage.” In reality, China is carrying out large-scale expansions to break away from the focus on mid-sized vessels and enter the high value-added vessel market. Hudong-Zhonghua Shipbuilding under the China State Shipbuilding Corporation (CSSC) has expanded a new dock and is about to start operation, and Hengli Heavy Industry and others are introducing an unconventional method of building vessels in advance and then selling them, while rapidly breaking down eco-friendly and high value-added technological barriers, such as being on the verge of delivering the world’s first ammonia-propelled bulk carrier. Market Share Gap with China Surges from 19%p to 62%p in 5 Years Amid this trend, the market share gap between the two countries in the entire global shipbuilding order market has widened dramatically. According to Clarkson Research, the order market share gap between South Korea and China was at the 19%p level just in 2021, but as of January to October this year, the gap between China (77%) and South Korea (15%) has expanded more than threefold in 5 years to a whopping 62%p. Experts warn that the sluggishness of the shipbuilding industry may not end simply as a crisis for a single industry but could lead directly to a crisis in national security and the maritime logistics supply chain. This is because the weakening of the domestic shipbuilding industry’s foundation can be a fatal blow even in terms of security infrastructure, which must timely procure and maintain naval power in case of an emergency. Domestic shipbuilders are staking their lives on improving their constitution to overcome the crisis. First, they are devoting efforts to securing source technologies for future zero-carbon vessels, including small modular reactor (SMR) propelled vessels, and are also accelerating the introduction of robots to maximize productivity and bridge the cost gap with China. For instance, HD Hyundai has presented a goal to introduce 3,000 robots into its shipyards by 2030. However, voices are loud that there is a clear limit to defending against China’s offensive backed by massive capital solely through the efforts of individual companies. The industry and academia agree that omnidirectional and multidimensional support at the government level is urgent, such as expanding smart vessel empirical test zones, easing regulations related to new technologies, and providing practical financial support. In some quarters, arguments are raised that a strategic collaboration system among the three major domestic companies is needed to counter rapidly growing Chinese shipbuilders, but the view also persists that realistic constraints are significant due to the interests and competitive dynamics of each company. Now that the reputation of a high value-added shipbuilding powerhouse is shaken, it is a golden time for the private sector, government, and academia to put their heads together and prepare an effective breakthrough. articles.title: CMA CGM strengthens partnership with Maritime Singapore
articles.summary: The CMA CGM Group is deepening its collaboration with Maritime Singapore in talent development, maritime innovation and sustainable shipping. The initiatives build on a long-standing relationship, including the Memorandum of Understanding with the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore, renewed in March 2025, which...
articles.body: The CMA CGM Group is deepening its collaboration with Maritime Singapore in talent development, maritime innovation and sustainable shipping. The initiatives build on a long-standing relationship, including the Memorandum of Understanding with the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore, renewed in March 2025, which covers decarbonisation, digitalisation and innovation. On talent, CMA CGM and the Singapore Maritime Foundation signed an MOU on 25 November 2026, in the presence of CMA CGM Chairman and CEO Rodolphe Saadé and Senior Minister of State Murali Pillai. CMA CGM will support MaritimeONE scholarships and internships for the next generation of maritime professionals. The two parties are exploring collaboration on MPA’s Maritime Leadership Programme in 2027. On innovation and digitalisation, CMA CGM’s accelerator ZEBOX, which supported the Smart Port Challenge in 2025 and 2026, signed a partnership agreement with PIER71 on 18 November 2026 to promote exchanges between startups, ease access to new markets and connect entrepreneurs with industry partners. MPA and CMA CGM have also trialled digital data exchange between ships and port authorities, using the APL SINGAPURA in 2025 and the CMA CGM GRAND PALAIS in 2026, to simplify port clearance and reduce manual processes. The findings will support a pilot in the first quarter of 2027. On alternative fuels, CMA CGM is evaluating prospective ethanol bunkering trials in Singapore to assess ethanol in marine engines and the related procedures, safety and operational requirements. MPA and CMA CGM are also exploring a near-term liquefied biomethane bunkering trial to examine how to account for and recognise the fuel’s sustainability benefits and emissions savings under different regulatory and voluntary frameworks. This builds on Singapore’s LNG bunkering capabilities, and CMA CGM regularly bunkers LNG there. On connectivity, CMA CGM’s intra-Asia specialist CNC introduced new services and enhanced existing ones in 2026, linking Singapore with Malaysia, Indonesia and Myanmar. MPA Chief Executive Ang Wee Keong said the partnership brings together complementary capabilities to meet the evolving needs of international shipping. Bo Wegener, CEO of CMA CGM Asia Pacific, called Singapore central to the company’s presence and ambitions in the region, and said the collaboration combines talent, innovation, digitalisation and new energy solutions to strengthen the industry’s resilience and competitiveness.

articles.title: MSC expands Asia service through the Northwest Seaport Alliance Gateway
articles.summary: The Northwest Seaport Alliance has welcomed Mediterranean Shipping Company’s enhancement of its Asia-Pacific Northwest network, which brings more service through the NWSA gateway and new cargo opportunities through Seattle. MSC is enhancing its Chinook Service and reinstating its Mustang Service, giving the region...
articles.body: The Northwest Seaport Alliance has welcomed Mediterranean Shipping Company’s enhancement of its Asia-Pacific Northwest network, which brings more service through the NWSA gateway and new cargo opportunities through Seattle. MSC is enhancing its Chinook Service and reinstating its Mustang Service, giving the region two dedicated loops that connect major Asian markets with broader coverage, greater flexibility and improved direct connectivity. The revised Chinook Service, starting in week 50, provides a link from South Vietnam to the gateway. Its eastbound rotation will call at Dong Nai, Xiamen, Shanghai, Qingdao, Busan, Vancouver, Seattle and Prince Rupert. MSC expects the shorter rotation, with fewer port calls and less time in port, to improve schedule reliability and provide competitive transit times. The Mustang Service will be reinstated from Yantian on 13 December 2026, rotating Yantian, Ningbo, Busan, Seattle and Vancouver. The additional Seattle call strengthens direct links between key Asian markets and the gateway, with cargo moving through Terminal 5 and onward by rail to the US Midwest and beyond, supported by the NWSA’s market-leading low import rail dwell on the West Coast. MSC’s wider network also includes the weekly California Express, which calls at Seattle and offers a Latin America connection through Mexico and Panama, along with direct access to Mediterranean markets. Together, the services widen the range of international markets reachable through the gateway and give beneficial cargo owners more options for moving goods through the Pacific Northwest. Dick Marzano, NWSA Co-Chair and Port of Tacoma Commission President, said Vietnam is an important and growing market and that the enhanced Chinook Service gives more reliable, efficient access between South Vietnam and the region. Ryan Calkins, NWSA Co-Chair and Port of Seattle Commission President, called the Mustang reinstatement, with Seattle as first port of call, a strong vote of confidence in the gateway, saying more service means more options for cargo owners and greater connectivity with important Asian trading markets.

articles.body: The Free Hanseatic City of Bremen and Uruguay’s National Port Administration have signed a joint Declaration of Intent in Montevideo on 21 November 2026 to develop their cooperation in port management, logistics and maritime trade. Kristina Vogt signed for the Bremen Senate and Stefan Färber for bremenports. The aim is to strengthen institutional ties and widen the exchange of knowledge, experience and best practice. The next step will be to establish a formal cooperation framework in the near future, in line with the legal and administrative requirements of both sides. Talks covered shore-side power, port energy supply, water depths, modernisation and digitalisation, with Uruguay generating almost all of its electricity from renewable sources and keen to build on that. Economic relations and markets were also a focus. Kristina Vogt, Senator for Ports, said the cooperation offers a chance to exchange experience and, where appropriate, offer services to one another, and that strategic partnerships with other regions are important. She said the declaration provides a solid base for developing the cooperation as quickly as possible. André Grobien, President of the Bremen Chamber of Commerce, said the agreement sends an important signal at the right time, as Bremen and Bremerhaven have a long-term interest in expanding economic ties with Uruguay and the MERCOSUR region and want to be seen as a reliable partner amid geopolitical change. Stefan Färber, Head of Port Development at bremenports, said Montevideo and the Bremen ports face very similar questions on decarbonising port operations, using digitalisation to improve efficiency, and building infrastructure for alternative fuels and climate-neutral shipping, which the partners intend to address together.

Amirhosein Khorgooi/ISNA/via WANA (West Asia News Agency) via REUTERS By Weilun Soon Nov 26, 2026 (Bloomberg) –Tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has risen this month, according to data from Vortexa , even as attacks on vessels in the contested waterway have increased. The number of ships carrying crude, fuels and liquefied natural gas stayed above 26, on a seven-day moving average basis, this month through Nov. 19, the figures show. That compares with October, when transits were below 25 on at least two-thirds of the days. The Vortexa data also show the amount of very large crude carriers and Suezmaxes crossing the strait has decreased slightly, while the number of smaller vessels has risen. This comes as oil-product tankers, which are smaller than crude carriers, are increasingly being converted to transport oil. The danger of shipping energy through Hormuz has increased in recent weeks. Iran has launched a wave of attacks on tankers, while widening the scope of vessels it says shouldn’t be transiting the waterway to include tugboats . Meanwhile, the cost to shuttle oil through the strait and additional insurance fees have also risen to near war-time highs, a reflection of the risks shipowners are taking to make the passage. The numbers, however, may not capture all of the vessels moving through Hormuz. Signal interference, spoofing and dark transits may affect real-time monitoring of data and the tally may be revised when more information becomes available, Vortexa said. © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. articles.summary: At least one crew member aboard a ship carrying diesel has died after the vessel capsized and partially sank off the Spanish island of Ibiza on Thursday, regional authorities said, adding there were no signs of pollution so far.

Spanish Transport Ministry/via Reuters TV/Handout via REUTERS THIS IMAGE HAS BEEN SUPPLIED BY A THIRD PARTY MADRID, Nov 26 (Reuters) – At least one crew member aboard a ship carrying diesel has died after the vessel capsized and partially sank off the Spanish island of Ibiza on Thursday, regional authorities said, adding there were no signs of pollution so far. The Malta-flagged chemical tanker Med Emre was sailing from Algeciras to Barcelona and may have been carrying up to 7,000 metric tons of diesel when it keeled over about 30 nautical miles (56 km) off Ibiza’s northwestern coast, the Balearic Islands’ interior department said. Emergency services said all 17 crew members were rescued, but one died after being taken directly to Ibiza’s Can Misses hospital. Six others were brought to Ibiza airport and taken to two hospitals with light injuries, primarily hypothermia. Of the remaining crew, five were taken to Valencia and five remained in good condition aboard a rescue vessel, they added. Pablo Garriz, the Balearic Islands’ regional head of emergencies, said the crew included Turkish and Indian nationals, but he could not yet confirm the nationality of the deceased. The tanker remained partially submerged with its keel protruding above the surface, Garriz told reporters, despite initial indications that it had sunk completely. “The positive news is that the vessel is not on the seabed but remains semi-submerged at the surface, which allows salvage and containment operations,” he said, adding there was currently no impact on Balearic waters or coastline and no evidence of a significant spill, although small sheens had been observed. Technical experts were assessing the vessel’s stability before deciding on salvage and cargo-recovery operations, he added. Spain’s maritime rescue service sent an aircraft and a vessel specialized in oil-spill response, the Clara Campoamor, to survey the area. Three helicopters took part in the rescue, along with nearby merchant vessels. Spain’s merchant marine authority activated the national maritime pollution contingency plan at level 2, the second-highest. The waters surrounding Ibiza are a habitat for sea turtles, dolphins and the Balearic shearwater, one of Europe’s most threatened seabirds. The area is also home to extensive meadows of Posidonia oceanica seagrass, which plays a vital role in supporting marine biodiversity. Spain’s worst maritime environmental disaster occurred in 2002, when the Bahamas-flagged tanker Prestige sank off the northwestern Galicia region, spilling tens of thousands of tons of heavy fuel oil and fouling hundreds of beaches in Spain and France. The Balearic regional government said it was gathering information on the accident and its possible consequences, including any risk of fuel pollution, before deciding on further measures. Designed to support environmental campaigns and scientific research worldwide while minimizing fossil fuel consumption…
articles.body: Freire Shipyard Celebrates Launch of New Greenpeace Vessel Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 25, 2026 © Greenpeace International Freire Shipyard celebrated the launch ceremony of NB 737 on November 25, 2026 in Vigo, marking a milestone in the construction of Greenpeace International's new flagship vessel. Designed to support environmental campaigns and scientific research worldwide while minimizing fossil fuel consumption, the vessel is scheduled for delivery by the end of 2027. With an overall length of 75 meters, the new sailing vessel has been designed to undertake demanding, long-range maritime operations, including campaigns in polar regions. Its design prioritizes energy efficiency, combining wind propulsion with an intelligent energy generation, storage and management system to minimize fossil fuel consumption. The vessel will feature a range of energy generation and storage technologies, including solar panels, battery storage systems, energy recovery systems and hydrogen fuel cells. These will be complemented by four dual-fuel internal combustion engine generator sets for electricity generation designed to use green methanol (MeOH) as their primary fuel, with small quantities of marine gas oil (MGO) used to initiate combustion. One of the key features of the design is the automated DynaRig sailing propulsion system, comprising two rotating masts with a combined sail area of 1,746 square meters. Under favorable weather conditions, this configuration will enable the vessel to circumnavigate the globe using wind power alone. In addition, while sailing, the propellers will be able to operate as generators, harnessing the vessel's movement to produce electricity. The aim is for the vessel to operate with minimal fossil fuel use from the outset, with a view to eliminating it entirely as the necessary supply chains and infrastructure become available. In addition, the vessel will feature onboard laboratories, systems for deploying remotely operated vehicles (ROVs) and autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs), a helideck equipped to support helicopter operations, and four auxiliary boats that can be deployed even in challenging sea conditions. With the addition of NB 737, Greenpeace will expand its fleet, which currently comprises the Rainbow Warrior Ill, the Arctic Sunrise and the Witness, further strengthening its capacity to carry out environmental campaigns and scientific research in defense of the environment.

articles.summary: The US announced plans to impose a fresh round of tariffs on goods from China, the European Union and a dozen other economies under President Donald Trump’s push to restore sweeping global import taxes that the Supreme Court found unconstitutional.

BRENDAN SMIALOWSKI/Pool via REUTERS/File Photo By Alicia Diaz (Bloomberg) –The US announced plans to impose a fresh round of tariffs on goods from China, the European Union and a dozen other economies under President Donald Trump’s push to restore sweeping global import taxes that the Supreme Court found unconstitutional. The rate for imports from China would rise to 20%, in line with the country’s prior agreement with the Trump administration — though that rate could double to 40% if talks between the two countries fall apart, according to a senior US official. The official briefed reporters on condition of anonymity ahead of Wednesday’s announcement. Products from the EU will be taxed at 15% in compliance with the US’s deal with the bloc, though that could also rise to as much as 20%, according to the Office of the US Trade Representative. Tariffs will apply to items from economies the Trump administration accuses of overproduction in some domestic industries and hurting American companies. They are still subject to a public comment process and could change. A final action could come as early as January, the official said. The new levies mark the latest effort by the administration to reinstate an expansive tariff agenda that included country-by-country levies implemented using emergency powers. Those were struck down by high-court justices in February, forcing Trump to invoke other legal authorities to advance his agenda. It’s a politically risky move. Democrats swept to a landslide victory in the midterm elections earlier this month thanks in part to voter anger over the cost of living and disapproval of the president’s handling of the economy. China and the EU could also retaliate, though initial signals from them were muted. Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun told a briefing earlier Wednesday that the prospect of new US tariffs on its exports was “political maneuvering” and said the two nations should work together to maintain their trade truce. The announcement appears to comply with the 2025 trade agreement between the US and EU, which capped tariffs at 15% on most of the bloc’s exports. As a result, the move likely won’t antagonize transatlantic relations for now. European Commission spokesman Olof Gill said “we strongly reject the premise that Europe is a source of structural overcapacity” and added the bloc expects new levies to abide by the tariff agreement. US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the new duties were designed to preserve existing deals while addressing overcapacity concerns. “A lot of these deals we made actually solve a lot of the problems we see in excess capacity or can go toward it,” Greer said Wednesday on CNBC. “We’ve talked to our trading partners about this. They know what we’re proposing. I think a lot of this is baked in.” Imports from Japan, South Korea, Switzerland — all prominent US trading partners — would be hit with a 15% rate. The number could go up to 25% for Korea and 20% for the other two, USTR said. Indian products would face a 17% charge if a trade pact with Washington is finalized, though that could increase to 25%. Several smaller nations in Asia were also hit. Similar expected measures aimed at Mexico and Norway were not included but remain under consideration, the official said. Greer said on CNBC the US has “had some very good conversations with Mexico” on the issue. The tariffs follow a probe that began in March into alleged excess manufacturing capacity, utilizing Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, a process seen as more resistant to legal challenges than Trump’s prior tariff wall. The tariff rates aren’t expected to surpass already agreed-upon levels in trade agreements with each economy. The move will test the tolerance of economic partners, who have largely held back from retaliating, opting instead to negotiate deals with the US to minimize their tariffs. That dynamic could be on display next month, when Trump meets again with his Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping, on the sidelines of the Group of 20 summit. Their trade truce is set to expire in January unless the two powers agree to extend it. “If we were to go beyond the 20% or something like that, they would view that as breaking our deal,” Greer said, The trade ambassador said Washington and Beijing are also “proposing to implement” tariff reductions under its new board of trade on around $30 billion of non-sensitive exports. Greer signaled that the new levy will not stack on top of existing duties of 10% or 12.5% under a separate investigation into negligent enforcement of forced-labor laws. “Those are not really additive,” he said on CNBC. For products eligible to be hit by both sets of duties, only the higher rate would apply, the official said earlier. The official added that there would be goods exempted from the tariffs, including oil and gas and food products that cannot be grown in the US. Other products that are already subject to sectoral duties, including tariffs on pharmaceuticals and critical minerals, are also exempted. After the Supreme Court loss, Trump immediately announced plans to rebuild his tariff wall under a different legal authority. Under the Section 301 framework, the president can implement tariffs following an investigation into allegedly unfair foreign trading practices. While Section 301 tariffs are seen as more legally sound and flexible than other powers Trump has eyed, they’re also more time-consuming. An earlier investigation under the same legal authority into policies around forced labor from US trading partners resulted in tariffs on some 60 economies. Those duties are currently facing legal challenges. The new tariffs apply to Bangladesh, Cambodia, China, the European Union, India, Indonesia, Japan, Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand, and Vietnam. USTR also announced it is raising tariffs on imports from Brazil, altering a previously-conducted trade investigation into the country’s digital policies and trade practices. The US is considering increasing the out-of-quota tariff rate on raw and refined sugar and proposing a 10% tariff on finished aircraft. The increased levy on imports from Brazil comes weeks after Trump ally Flavio Bolsonaro lost his presidential election bid to progressive incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. articles.summary: The International Maritime Organization (IMO) is calling on shipping companies to make more training berths available to cadets, highlighting a longstanding disconnect between the industry’s need for qualified seafarers and...

Join the leading maritime news network Photo courtesy IMO The International Maritime Organization (IMO) is calling on shipping companies to make more training berths available to cadets, highlighting a longstanding disconnect between the industry’s need for qualified seafarers and the lack of opportunities for young people to gain the sea time required to enter the profession. In many developing countries, aspiring officers complete their shore-based maritime education only to spend years waiting for an onboard training placement, even as shipping companies struggle to recruit qualified personnel. In an announcement Tuesday, the IMO outlined efforts to expand its NextWave Seafarers initiative, which aims to address the bottleneck through cooperation between governments, shipowners and maritime training institutions. More than 80 participants representing over 25 countries gathered at IMO headquarters in London on November 20 to formally launch the second phase of the initiative and explore ways to increase the availability of onboard training opportunities. The program’s pilot phase, developed in partnership with Saudi Arabia’s Transport General Authority and national shipping company Bahri, saw 19 cadets from developing island nations and least developed countries complete their onboard training aboard Bahri vessels. The second phase aims to train at least 30 additional cadets, with women accounting for half of participants. The IMO also wants to recruit at least five shipping companies to provide training berths, laying the groundwork for a wider international partnership. The workshop examined practical barriers to cadet placements, including visa restrictions complicating crew changes, as well as the importance of providing a safe and supportive working environment for young seafarers entering the industry. The shortage of training berths exposes a fundamental challenge in addressing the industry’s workforce needs. Expanding maritime education alone will do little to increase the supply of qualified officers if graduates cannot secure the mandatory sea time needed to earn their professional credentials. Without sufficient participation from shipowners, the industry risks leaving a pool of prospective seafarers untapped at a time when it needs to attract and retain the next generation of maritime professionals. articles.title: Red Sea and Indian Ocean Nations Advance Plans for Combined Maritime Security Force
articles.summary: Countries bordering the Red Sea and Western Indian Ocean are moving toward establishing a combined maritime task force to combat piracy, strengthen regional security and protect commercial shipping across some...

Join the leading maritime news network An EUNAVFOR warship escorts a CMA CGM containership in the Red Sea as part of the EU's Operation ASPIDES. Photo courtesy EUNAVFOR Countries bordering the Red Sea and Western Indian Ocean are moving toward establishing a combined maritime task force to combat piracy, strengthen regional security and protect commercial shipping across some of the world’s most strategically important waterways. The International Maritime Organization (IMO) announced that signatories to the Djibouti Code of Conduct and its Jeddah Amendment have adopted a new Regional Maritime Security Strategy and agreed to advance plans for a Combined Maritime Task Force (CMTF). The agreement was reached during a high-level meeting held November 11–13 in Antananarivo, Madagascar. The proposed task force would build on existing national and regional maritime security capabilities, improving coordination among participating countries. Governments agreed to develop the force’s legal framework and concept of operations in 2027. The initiative comes amid persistent threats to commercial shipping in the Red Sea and renewed concerns over piracy off the Horn of Africa, underscoring the need for greater regional cooperation in protecting international trade and seafarers. The broader security strategy covers the Western Indian Ocean, Gulf of Aden and Red Sea. Preparatory work began in Saudi Arabia in November 2024, with government representatives, navies, coast guards and maritime law enforcement agencies subsequently meeting in Mombasa, Kenya, earlier this month to finalize the framework. Originally adopted in 2009 in response to Somali piracy, the Djibouti Code of Conduct was expanded in 2017 through the Jeddah Amendment to address a wider range of maritime security threats. Somalia’s Minister of State Mohamed Abdulkadir Mohamed emphasized the human cost of attacks on commercial shipping during the meeting. “The protection of seafarers is not simply a maritime security obligation; it is a fundamental humanitarian responsibility,” he said. The meeting also marked a leadership milestone, with Tanzania’s Stella Katondo becoming the first woman elected to chair the regional initiative. South Africa will serve as deputy chair. While the agreement represents a significant step toward a more coordinated regional security presence, the proposed task force remains in development. The IMO has not announced a deployment timeline or details of participating naval assets. Finnish Border Guard/Handout via REUTERS ROME, Nov 25 (Reuters) – Italy has told Ukraine it was wrong to attack Russian ships in Libyan waters and warned Kyiv not to spread the war to new areas, Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani told Corriere della Sera newspaper on Wednesday. “It was a mistake to violate Libya’s sovereignty,” Tajani said, adding that Rome had received no advance warning of the Ukrainian operations. “Italy was absolutely unaware of Kyiv’s intentions to strike in Libyan territorial waters, even inside a port,” said the minister, who is head of the coalition Forza Italia party. Ukraine has said the maritime drone attack against a Russian naval corvette and a cargo ship at the weekend was a legitimate act of self-defence. Tajani said he had telephoned his Ukrainian counterpart, Andrii Sybiha, to express his concerns, stressing Italy’s commitment to Libya’s territorial integrity. Another coalition party, the far-right League, also condemned the attack, calling it “unacceptable” and warning that it risked destabilising the north African country. Italy has been a staunch supporter of Ukraine since Russia’s 2022 invasion, providing military aid and backing European sanctions against Moscow. However, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s government has sent mixed signals, with her own party firmly behind Kyiv while the League, led by Matteo Salvini, has repeatedly criticised continued military assistance to Ukraine. Tajani said that Rome would carry on supporting Kyiv’s sovereignty while seeking to prevent the conflict from spreading. “Italy will remain on Ukraine’s side. Ours is a strategic choice,” he said. articles.title: Canary Islands Receive Recording-Breaking Number of Migrants In Single Day
articles.summary: A record 2,100-plus migrants arrived in Spain's Canary Islands over 24 hours in overcrowded boats, maritime rescue service data showed on Wednesday, prompting regional leader Fernando Clavijo to call for a European-level response to the crisis."The Canaries can't take it anymore.
articles.body: Canary Islands Receive Recording-Breaking Number of Migrants In Single Day Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 25, 2026 © Adobe Stock/Halina A record 2,100-plus migrants arrived in Spain's Canary Islands over 24 hours in overcrowded boats, maritime rescue service data showed on Wednesday, prompting regional leader Fernando Clavijo to call for a European-level response to the crisis. "The Canaries can't take it anymore. We're experiencing an unprecedented migration pressure," Clavijo wrote on X, adding that he had requested an urgent meeting with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. "These people come to Europe and it's not fair that we alone respond to a drama of this magnitude," he said. One migrant was found dead in a boat and another gave birth during the perilous crossing from West Africa, the rescue service said. The daily arrivals surpassed the previous record of about 1,500 set two weeks ago. Most of the boats arrived at El Hierro, an island of some 11,400 residents that has become one of Europe's key entry points for migrants from West Africa. Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, who has faced tough criticism of his open stance on migration during the campaign ahead of Sunday's parliamentary election, said on Wednesday Europe needed a comprehensive approach to migration, including stronger border controls in cooperation with Senegalese and Gambian authorities. Still, he said Spain needed "to open legal migration pathways" for workers in sectors such as housing that are short of qualified labour. The Atlantic route from West Africa to the Canary Islands is one of the world's deadliest migration crossings as migrants seek to reach Spanish territory despite rough seas, strong currents and long distances. Arrivals tend to pick up in the autumn months, when sea conditions along the route are generally calmer and more favourable for crossings. Arrivals so far this year had climbed to 28,103 as of late November, more than last year's total but still well below an all-time high of 46,843 recorded in 2024, when most crossings occurred during the first nine months of the year. Nearly 21,000 people have reached the archipelago in the last two months. (Reuters)
